newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban forced on to defensive, but remain potent.
newsitem.headline: Taleban forced on to defensive, but remain potent.

text.p: The tide that propelled the purist Islamic Taleban militia to fleeting control of nine-tenths of Afghanistan has broken on the rocks of northern resistance.
The militia's defeats in the north in recent weeks have restored the military balance, but there is no sign yet that the two sides have fought themselves to a standstill.

"Militarily, it could still go either way," said a Western defence analyst, who asked not to be named. "The Taleban have logistic support and reinforcements, even though these are untrained kids. They have the upper hand in holding strategic points like Kabul, but have to divert energy and manpower to administering and maintaining security in the large parts of the country they hold," he said.

"The northern factions have seized the military initiative, but can only count on a finite reserve of troops and unknown logistical support. So it's fairly even," he added. When the northern town of Pul-i-Khumri fell on Wednesday, the Taleban lost the last of the territory they had grabbed after an opposition commander changed sides last month.

The frontlines are now back where they were in January, with opposition forces entrenched in the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush range, holding the central province of Bamiyan and contesting the remote northwestern province of Badghis.

By Thursday, opposition commander Ahmad Shah Masood had led his battle-hardened guerrillas to within a few km (miles) of the Soviet-built Bagram airbase, 50 km (31 miles) from Kabul. The changing military equation has prompted political responses in both camps, but no real readiness for peace talks.

Wakil Ahmad, a senior Taleban official in the southern city of Kandahar, noted bitterly that it was negotiations, not military victory, which had brought Taleban forces to the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif three weeks ago.

They had barely 72 hours to savour their triumph before their new ally, General Abdul Malik, who had ousted opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, changed sides again. His ethnic Uzbek troops and fighters of the Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat party rose against the mainly ethnic Pashtun newcomers and drove them from the city in battles that cost the Taleban an estimated 300 dead and hundreds more captured.
"In the light of these events, negotiations with the opposition are not useful," Ahmad said on Saturday. "We have seen there is no honesty or sincerity on their side."
The Taleban also suffered the psychological blow of losing many of their leaders.

Their foreign minister, northern military chief and central bank governor were believed to have been captured in Mazar-i-Sharif. Their information and interior ministers were in the Taleban force that fled from Pul-i-Khumri.
The Taleban's reclusive supreme leader, Mullah Mohammad Omar, has spent the past week in Kabul, on his first visit since his forces seized it in September, to boost sagging morale.
One result was the appointment of Mullah Abdul Jalil to replace the captive Mullah Mohammad Ghous as foreign minister.

Opposition Uzbek, Tajik and Shi'ite Hazara forces, who have little in common apart from a shared fear of the Taleban, have also been struggling to forge a more cohesive alliance. "The Shi'ites are particularly worried," said an Afghan watcher in Mazar-i-Sharif. "They feel the most threatened by the (Sunni Moslem) Taleban because of their religious differences and they are not sure how far they can trust Malik, who after all invited the Taleban into the north."

The anti-Taleban alliance, which includes Malik's Junbish-i-Milli faction, the Jamiat-i-Islami party led by ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani, and Hezb-i-Wahdat agreed on Thursday to set up a new provisional government.
Rabbani said after talks with Malik on Saturday that technocrats would replace guerrilla faction leaders in the government, but stressed there would be no change at the top.
"There is a need for some changes in the government, but the leadership of the Islamic State will remain the same," he said.

For the moment, U.N. officials see little prospect of starting a serious dialogue among the belligerents. But Pakistan, widely derided for recognising the Kabul government just before the Taleban debacle in the north, has announced ambitious plans to host what amounts to an international peace conference on Afghanistan.

Islamabad proposed on Friday that the United States and Russia guarantee decisions that may be taken in the talks, to which it plans to invite warring Afghan factions as well as Afghanistan's immediate neighbours -- Iran, Pakistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
